entries.title: How to find the best Black Friday deals and shop smarter
entries.summary: Collage of various holiday shopping products
entries.content:
Between flash sales, doorbusters, and dozens of open browser tabs, holiday deal-hunting can take up all your time. Our shopping features are here to lend a hand, helping you save time and money. Here are four ways to snag the best deals and gifts this Black Friday and Cyber Monday.

1. Prep your wish list and snag deals with Universal Cart.

Universal Cart can act as your central game plan for Black Friday and Cyber Monday. Add items you’re eyeing across retailers into one organized place, Universal Cart will notify you about price drops or when out-of-stock items return. It also shows you merchant promo codes and offers.

The cart is built on Google Wallet so it understands your card perks and intelligently helps you choose between payment methods. When you’re ready to buy, check out securely right in the cart using Google Pay, or transfer your items to the retailer’s site to check out there.

2. Find gifts for anyone on your list with Search and the Gemini app.

Shopping for friends and family who have niche hobbies or never share a wishlist can leave you stuck for ideas. With AI Mode in Search or the Gemini app, just describe the person you’re shopping for in everyday language like “useful gifts under $40 for an uncle training for his first half marathon” to get tailored thought starters and gift ideas with customer reviews, photos, and store availability.

3. Shop with confidence using Price Insights.

Before you click “check out,” make sure you have the best deals out there. Tap the product listing on Google to compare prices across merchants and review price history to see whether the price is low, typical, or high. If you want to know when the price drops, tap “Track price” or ask AI Mode to let you know when there’s a deal.

4. Search in-store shelves using Google Lens.

If an item on a store shelf catches your eye, you do not have to guess what to type into Search to find it online. Just open up the Google app (Android and iOS), tap the Lens camera icon and snap a photo to instantly learn more about the product and see everything from customer reviews to product details to similar styles. You can even ask follow-up questions about what you see, like “does this come in navy blue?” or “what’s a great complimentary gift to go with this?”

With Google tools helping you tackle your holiday gift shopping, you can check your list off early and spend more time celebrating with family and friends.

entries.title: New Ask Maps features to help with holiday travel and prep
entries.content:
The holidays are a busy time between shopping for gifts, planning travel, and celebrating with loved ones. To help you stay one step ahead this season, we’re launching new Ask Maps features that make it easy to create itineraries, find available appointments, and search your lists in a snap so you can enjoy stress-free festivities.

Get on-the-go help with your holiday road trips

Now you can build step-by-step trip itineraries and get helpful, real-time details about your route right when you pull up directions.

Use Ask Maps to plan a day trip for holiday shopping or something more complex — like a three-day road trip with stops for coastal hikes and oceanfront dining. You'll get a day-by-day schedule with insider tips and numbered map pins for each stop, making it easy to visualize the plan. Once you're happy with the itinerary, share it with friends and family, or export it to Google Docs on desktop.

When you’re about to head out, use Ask Maps to pull up your itinerary or look for the “itinerary” badge in your chat history. You’ll see real-time details like live traffic conditions, whether a place is open, and even what the vibe is at your next stop. You can also adjust your schedule on the fly. Just use Ask Maps to add a scenic viewpoint or lunch spot along the way. Then, tap to get directions to your next stop right from your itinerary.

Whether you're taking a multi-day road trip or running errands around town, Maps keeps you a step ahead. Pull up directions to see helpful “Know before you go” tips about your route, including where to park or charge your car, and real-time conditions like weather, potential delays, and tolls.

Check off your holiday prep and let Maps find appointments for you

Holiday prep comes with a long list of to-dos. Now, with new agentic capabilities, you can choose to have Ask Maps find beauty, pet care, auto and home repair appointments online and call local businesses for you. Just ask, “Find me a 4 p.m. nail appointment near me.” Ask Maps will show you open slots across nearby businesses so it’s easy to decide what to book.

Show your guests the best spots on your lists

If you have friends visiting and want to show them around, now you can use Ask Maps to find saved places on your lists in seconds. Just ask, “Which spots saved in my lists have availability for five people in the next 30 minutes?” Ask Maps looks across your lists and checks live availability so you can pick a place and go.

These updates start rolling out today on Android and iOS just in time for the holidays. As part of today’s news, Ask Maps starts expanding to 30 countries across Europe — including Spain, Germany, and the U.K. — bringing Ask Maps to more than 200 countries and territories globally.

Travel itineraries and list search are available everywhere Ask Maps is offered. "Know before you go" route tips and finding appointments are launching first in the U.S., with more regions coming soon.

entries.title: Navigate holiday traffic and crowds with Google Maps trends
entries.summary: The illustration shows a woman using a Google Maps on a phone.
entries.content:
Nothing tests your holiday cheer quite like sitting in a two-mile highway standstill. But with a little strategic timing — and a peek into Google Maps trends — you can dodge the worst traffic jams, skip the grocery store lines, and get straight to the good parts of the holiday.

Beat the holiday traffic

If you’re driving for Thanksgiving, timing is everything. Here’s when to hit the road — and when to stay put:

  • Heading to Thanksgiving dinner: Roads are generally quiet on Thanksgiving Day, particularly after 12 p.m. Hit the road by early afternoon to make it on time for dinner.
  • Best times for long-distance travel: Aim for before 9 a.m. or after 6 p.m. on Wednesday, or before 1 p.m. and after 6 p.m. on Tuesday. Better yet, depart early on Sunday or Monday to avoid heavy congestion.
  • Worst times to travel: Avoid leaving between noon and 3 p.m. on Wednesday, or 3 p.m. and 5 p.m. on Tuesday. Watch out for the Friday before Thanksgiving as well — traffic peaks between 3 p.m. and 5 p.m.
  • Black Friday driving: Expect the heaviest traffic between 11 a.m. and 3 p.m.
  • Returning home: Start your trip back before noon or after 3 p.m. on Sunday.

Dodge the crowds

Between holiday prep and entertaining, places around town can get packed. Here are the best times to tackle your errands and skip the lines:

  • Grocery stores: Crowds peak the weekend before Thanksgiving at around 2 p.m. on Saturday and Sunday. For shorter lines, shop before 4 p.m. from Monday through Wednesday.
  • Bakeries: Avoid the rush at 11 a.m. Saturday before Thanksgiving. Instead, visit before noon Monday through Wednesday.
  • Movie theaters: The busiest showtimes fall around 7 p.m. on the Saturdays before and after Thanksgiving. Head to a movie before 5 p.m. on Black Friday for a quieter trip.

Hit up top holiday spots

These are some of the highly-rated destinations that see the biggest spikes in interest across the country this time of year:

  • Christmas In The Park, San Jose, CA
  • Louisville Mega Cavern, Louisville, KY
  • Wollman Rink, New York, NY
  • Vitruvian Park, Dallas, TX
  • Rockefeller Center, New York, NY

Need more holiday help? See how our latest updates to Ask Maps can help you plan the perfect itinerary, conquer holiday appointments, and more. Wherever your holiday plans take you, Google Maps is here to help you get there with less stress.

entries.title: 4 ways Search can help with your holiday plans
entries.summary: Illustration showing holiday items like presents and candy canes, with search for how to build a gingerbread house
entries.content:
Preparing a family feast, setting a festive scene, or making travel plans can quickly crowd your calendar. If you’re looking to simplify your holiday prep, Search is ready to handle the heavy lifting. Here are four ways Search can help tackle your seasonal to-do list.

Rescue kitchen mishaps in real time with Search Live

Imagine you're making a chocolate ganache for your holiday party, and instead of a glossy glaze, you’re staring at a curdled mess. To get help in the moment, tap the Live icon in the Google app (available on Android and iOS), turn on your video, and point your camera at the mixing bowl. You can then use your voice to ask Search if the chocolate is salvageable and get instructions for an easy fix, along with links to explore further.

Recreate holiday decor with Lens in Search

When you spot holiday decor inspiration, like an eye-catching tablescape at a local restaurant or a festive design online, Lens helps you bring the look home. Open the Google app, tap the Lens camera icon in the Search bar, and snap a photo or upload a screenshot (on Android, you can also use Circle to Search). Then ask, “help me find the pieces to recreate this tablescape for my holiday party next weekend.”

Search breaks down the scene into individual elements and shows you shoppable links and local in-stock options, so you can easily put the look together yourself.

Book your holiday getaway with AI Mode in Search

If you'd rather travel (or book a staycation) for the holidays, AI Mode in Search can map out your trip and take care of reservations. To find a place to stay, describe your destination, dates, and preferences — like a cozy fireplace or boutique vibe.

You’ll get a visual list of options to compare amenities, guest reviews, and photos. When you're ready to reserve your room, you can click out to book directly with travel partners — or, if you see “Continue on Google,” complete your hotel reservation right in AI Mode using Google Pay. 1

Once your room is set, you can lock in dinner plans without switching apps. Just tell AI Mode what you're craving, along with party size and preferred time. Search pulls together available tables that match your criteria, so you can quickly complete the booking. 2

Find holiday event tickets and track sold-out shows

Want to round out your holiday evening with a show? Just like booking dinner, you can use AI Mode in Search to find and compare event tickets. Describe what you want to see, along with your budget and dates, and Search pulls together options across ticketing partners so you can reserve seats in a few taps.

If a performance is sold out — or tickets haven't officially gone on sale yet — skip manually refreshing websites. Instead, put Search’s info monitoring capabilities to work and get the latest updates right when they’re available. Just set up a task, like: “keep me updated as soon as any NYC opera shows release their under 40 discounted tickets.”

Search will track ticket drops and price changes behind the scenes. The moment new tickets are announced, you’ll receive a notification from the Google app so you can grab your seats before they sell out.

No matter how you celebrate this year, we hope Search helps take a few things off your plate, leaving you more time to enjoy the magic with family and friends.

entries.title: What teenagers really think about online safety and AI
entries.content:
Read the Future Report and you meet a generation that is curious, capable and far more thoughtful about technology than we often give them credit for. Of the 6,000 UK teenagers surveyed, 77% said they always or often stop to consider whether what they find online can be trusted. That should make us optimistic, and it should inform how we think about keeping them safe.

Too often, public debates frame young people's digital lives as problems to be solved. Screen time to cut, platforms to restrict, harms to count. The report describes teenagers who are "digitally confident, curious and optimistic" while staying alert to the risks. That is much closer to what we hear from parents, who know what a great generation they are raising. They have concerns, but they also see children who are creative, funny and often remarkably sensible online. If policy starts only from fear, we risk designing for the worst case and failing everyone else.

When we think about online safety, we usually list what we hope to prevent. The risks are real, and parents are right to want them gone. But there is a second list we rarely write down and that one includes what gets lost when we take access away. The learning, the creativity, the conversations and the confidence that come from using technology well.

Those skills need to be developed over time in age appropriate ways. Knowing to check what you're consuming online is something that is learned through practice and with support. Trying things, getting some wrong, and working out what to do differently builds resilience. You can see it grow with age. The report tells us that 52% of 16 to 18 year olds always check what they find, compared with 33% of 13 to 15 year olds.

That learning takes place with the help, guidance, and involvement of parents and teachers Eighty-one percent of teens say they would ask a parent for help with misinformation, scams or cyberbullying, and that barely drops as they get older (83% of 13 to 15s, 79% of 16 to 18s). Teens want their parents involved with three in ten saying that parental supervision helps them get the balance right.

The same goes for AI. Two thirds of teens use it at least a couple of times a week, for creative projects (67%) or learning (65%). What's striking is how they use it. They value AI when it helps them understand, not just when it gives answers. One 15-year-old in the report said she needs to know "how it's been worked out" for her schoolwork. That is exactly the instinct parents and educators want to develop.

If we can, the opportunities are incredible. Older teens are already using AI to learn a language (20%), teach themselves to code (19%) and prepare for job applications (17%). This is a generation using technology to stretch themselves, and as an organisation dedicated to improving outcomes for children that’s exciting to read.

There is clearly more work to be done. The report is honest about the gap teenagers perceive. Twenty-six percent of older teens worry their parents can't recognise AI or fake content. Parents need to be brought on the journey to an AI enabled world alongside everyone else. They need platforms that are safe by design, the confidence to respond calmly when things go wrong, and the chance to learn about AI alongside their children.

This generation is giving us real reasons to be hopeful. Our job is to make sure every child gets to build these skills, with the adults in their lives beside them.

entries.title: Helping teens navigate online news and information
entries.summary: Internet Matters logo on green background.
entries.content:
Online spaces are where children and young people discover new ideas, keep up with current events, and learn about the world around them. This is highlighted in Google’s The Future Report, which gathered the views of 6,000 UK teenagers to better understand the opportunities and challenges that technology presents for young people.

For many (83%), information comes through algorithm-driven recommendations — which children see as positive for introducing them to new ideas they may not see otherwise. Young people are also increasingly accessing video-based content and prefer this for building understanding, particularly of difficult topics. They are also engaging with AI, using tools like AI chatbots for creativity and learning on a daily basis.

While the report highlights the positive ways in which the internet is used for discovery and learning, it also points to the challenges young people face in accessing high-quality, trustworthy information. Teens recognised that the proliferation of AI-generated and manipulated content was making the online information environment increasingly complex to navigate. This is echoed in Internet Matters’ own research, which found that the growth of this content is leaving children feeling less trusting of the news they encounter in their feeds and more concerned about their ability to distinguish between what is true and false online.

Addressing these challenges will be essential if we are to preserve the educational benefits of online spaces. Children and young people must have access to high-quality, accurate content, alongside the skills to critically engage in an increasingly complex information environment. This is especially important in the UK, which is set to lower the voting age to 16, with the aim of increasing lifelong democratic participation. However, this will only be possible if young people feel equipped to engage confidently with the news, politics and current affairs they encounter online.

Encouragingly, Google’s research found that many teenagers are already using strategies to verify online information, including cross-checking sources (49%), checking the credibility of websites and authors (48%) and speaking to parents and trusted adults about the content they have seen online (45%). However, the responsibility for navigating a changing and complex information environment should not rest with young people alone.

Platforms, educators, and policymakers all have a role to play in helping children and young people access trustworthy information and develop digital and media literacy. Schools must be supported with clear direction set by government, alongside the resources and training needed to teach these skills effectively in the classroom. Tech companies also have an important role to play by making their platforms and services safe and media-literate by design. This means supporting children to have age-appropriate experiences and embedding features that help young people evaluate, question and contextualise what they see.

Parents will also continue to be children’s main source of information about online safety, and who they turn to when they need support. Yet they are also navigating many of the same challenges as their children. As a result, we must ensure that they too feel confident and able to support children — whether this is through building their own media literacy skills, improving access to easy-to-use parental controls or providing advice on where to access high-quality content.

Through this shared approach, we can build a safer and more empowering digital environment where every young person can confidently participate and thrive.

entries.title: Listening to teens on online safety
entries.content:
Childnet has worked towards making the internet a great and safe place for over 30 years; however, it feels like concerns around online safety have never been higher. Whilst these conversations around online safety are happening, it is crucial that children and young people’s perspectives are taken into account.

At Childnet, youth voice is at the heart of everything we do, and we pride ourselves on not just listening to young people, but having their opinions shape everything we do. Young people tell us they believe that change is needed online and that significantly more needs to be done to make the online world a safe and positive space.

Why we need to listen to young people

Google’s The Future Report, which spoke to more than 6,000 UK teenagers, found that 67% use AI tools creatively daily. This mass adoption of this technology is very much in line with our own research released in February for Safer Internet Day 2026, which found that nearly all young people aged 8 to 17 (97%) use AI tools, with 58% saying that AI makes their lives better.

Our research found that young people liked to use AI for a variety of reasons, with 71% of young people saying that AI saves them a lot of time, while a growing number are using it for help and support, with 64% agreeing that AI is the best way to get advice quickly.

Both pieces of work show that young people are aware of the risks or challenges which come with spending time online, and of the impact of an overreliance on AI and other emerging technologies.

We found that 41% of teens feel like people their age are relying heavily on AI for emotional support or help with emotional issues, while almost one in seven (14%) say they use AI tools to discuss things they don’t feel they can talk to anyone else about. This could also be seen across The Future report, where almost a fifth (18%) of teens surveyed (and 20% of 16-18s) reported chatting to AI "as a friend".

We also can’t ignore the real fears that young people have shared about AI, with 60% of young people saying they are concerned about someone using AI to make inappropriate pictures of them, as well as concerns around the impact on creativity and schoolwork, and even for emotional support or friendship.

Through our work in schools, our youth advisory boards, and in our focus groups, we see time and time again that young people are not only willing to have conversations about their life online, but that they are eager to have their voices heard about the issues that matter most to them.

The role of parents and carers

Parents and carers play a key role in supporting their children online. Our research found that 74% of young people would talk to a parent or carer if they were worried about AI; however parents and carers need more support and resources too. Less than 1 in 5 parents have set rules or guidelines for how their child can use AI at home and only 13% know where to go for advice or support if they are worried about their child’s use of AI.

The Future report also showed young people who were willing to have these conversations with their parents and carers. Approximately three in ten teens indicated that allowing their parents to supervise their online activities (30%) was a helpful measure.

At Childnet, we have a range of free resources to help parents, carers, and educators have conversations with young people about their life online, including our Family Agreement, conversation starters, and youth voice in online safety toolkit. We also have specific resources designed to talk about AI, both in the classroom and at home.

There is a feeling of a state of flux, of often rapid change, in both technology and the rules around access to technology – in this context, education and conversations which take on board young people’s experience will be more important than ever.

entries.title: Claim your Google Cloud Credits in Google AI Studio
entries.summary: Google Cloud Credits in AI Studio
entries.content:
When you’re deep in a session in Google AI Studio — testing complex prompts with frontier models like gemini-4-carbon, generating videos with Omni, or building an app — you shouldn’t have to bounce across three websites just to set up billing and claim credits when you hit a quota limit.

Starting today, you can claim and manage free API credits directly inside AI Studio. That means you can create your Developer Program profile, link billing, and track your balance, all without leaving your workspace.

If you’re a Google AI Pro or Google AI Ultra subscriber, your membership already comes with recurring monthly Google Cloud credits through the Google Developer Program.

The Google Developer Program is a no-cost membership unifying tools, learning paths, and perks across AI Studio, Google Cloud, Firebase, Android, and more. An active profile is required for Google AI Pro and Ultra subscribers to access developer benefits like monthly Google Cloud credits, higher Google Antigravity quotas, and Google Skills credits. If you don’t have a profile, the new workflow in AI Studio automatically creates one when you redeem your credits.

Check the monthly credits included in your Google AI plan

Google AI Pro and Ultra plans include recurring monthly Google Cloud credits that you can put straight toward Gemini API usage for prompting, building, and deploying AI-powered apps from Google AI Studio. As detailed in our guide to using Google AI plan credits in AI Studio, your monthly credit grant scales with your AI plan tier.

Here’s how your monthly credits work over time.

  • 12-month rolling validity: Each monthly credit is valid for 12 months from issue.
  • Automatic monthly rollover: Grants stack month to month. If you’ve been a Pro or Ultra subscriber for a few months and have a Google Developer Program profile, you likely have credits waiting to be claimed.
  • Support for paid-tier models and overages: Use credits when your subscription quota runs out in AI Studio to keep creating generative media, solving complex tasks, or building 3D worlds with models like Gemini 4 Carbon. Upgrading your Google AI plan automatically increases your monthly grant.
  • Gemini API prepayment requirement: Using the Gemini API with Cloud billing requires a $5 minimum prepayment and balance in order to draw down promotional credits.
  • Primary subscriber exclusivity: Only the primary plan subscriber can use these credits. They can’t be shared among family members.

Claim and link your credits in a single click

  • Automatic credit alerts: Spot unclaimed credits and current balances right in the left nav on sign-in.
  • In-product redemption: Create your Google Developer Program profile and claim credits in one dialog.
  • Seamless billing setup and auto-apply: Set up a Cloud billing account within the same flow, spend earliest-expiring credits first, and auto-apply future monthly grants.
  • Instant paid API keys and spend tracking: Attach paid-tier API keys upon credit redemption and track your remaining balance and usage at aistudio.google.com/billing.

Get started today

Whether you’re generating with your first Gemini API key, vibe coding a full-stack application, or deploying to production with Google Cloud Run, your Google AI subscription now gives you an instant head start. Head to Google AI Studio to start building today.

entries.title: Connect Google Wallet to Gemini for personal finance insights
entries.content:
Personal Intelligence in Gemini securely connects information from apps you already use — like Gmail, Photos, YouTube, and Search — to make your experience more personalized and helpful. Today, we’re adding Google Wallet to the list of connected apps so you can get more tailored responses around personal finance.

Understand and plan your finances with Google Wallet

Rolling out today for all Gemini app users in the U.S., you can connect Google Wallet for responses informed by your spending habits. You also have the option to securely link your financial accounts from your credit cards and banks to Wallet via Plaid to unlock deeper insights.

Jump into Gemini and tag @Google Wallet to ask questions around personal finance, budgeting and more. Here are some things to try:

  • Visualize spending: Questions like “can we review my spending from last quarter so I can save $1,000 over the next three months?” enable Gemini to generate dynamic charts tracking cash flow, asset allocation, and budgets directly in your chat.
  • Find forgotten subscriptions: If you ask "what subscriptions am I still paying for, and did any of them go up in price this year?" Gemini finds recurring charges across your linked accounts and flags price increases.
  • Budget for the holidays: When you ask "how much did I spend on gifts and travel last year? Use that to help me set a holiday budget for this year," Gemini will look at your transactions from the last year and suggest a budget tailored to you.

Google Wallet in Gemini is rolling out across web and mobile, for Gemini app users on both Android and iOS.

Stay in control

We’ve built these tools with security and privacy at the center. If you choose to connect your Wallet (under Connected Apps in Personal Intelligence settings), Gemini can only read information from your accounts; it can’t move, manage, or invest your money. You decide if and when you want to opt in to this experience, and you can turn the connection on or off at any time. Learn more here.

For Personal Intelligence, we’re also making it easier for you to see and edit what Gemini remembers. Memory Summary gives you a clear, readable snapshot of your saved preferences, interests, and ongoing goals in one place so you always know how Gemini tailors responses for you. You can review and edit anytime. Open Profile > Personal Intelligence > Memory Summary to view, refine, or remove any details whenever you want. Memory Summary is available on web and mobile for all Gemini app users where Personal Intelligence is available.
